cells.tense: The clarity is here now, and it moves at the speed decisions actually need.
cells.ask: Name the one thing you're ending this week, write it in a sentence, and put the date under it. That's the whole act.
cells.core:
Deciding has stopped being a negotiation. Something in you has the answer before the discussion starts, and it doesn't need to argue its case — the call goes one way and the people around you feel the floor stop shifting. That steadiness is doing more than you're giving it credit for.

Where this has room is the not-knowing right before a call. Because the answer comes early, there's a gap you can afford to sit in a beat before you speak. Then say the ending out loud, plainly, to the one person it touches. Saying it is the part that keeps this steady, and saying it is the part that's yours to practice. Put a date on it.
cells.sheetLine: You're already deciding this. Say it plainly to one person.
cells.verb: deciding it through, finishing the thing rather than declaring it
cells.place: the room where something ends so the next can start

cells.tense: You're already standing at the far end of this ending, arranging a room nobody has cleared yet.
cells.ask: Before you decide anything else about this, write down what's actually true today. Today only, no projection.
cells.core:
You're several moves past the present, bracing for a future you can't write yet. Something ends, you've already run the next part in your head, and you keep pushing the people involved toward a conclusion they haven't reached. The push is doing the deciding for them, and it's costing you the ending itself.

What's underneath is honest — you're trying to protect something, or make it safe early. But a decision made ahead of the ground it stands on doesn't hold; people feel the hurry and dig in. Slow to the actual day. Let the ending finish before you start the next one, and let the pattern you're so good at seeing wait until there's something real to see it in.

cells.tense: The thing ended a while back, and you're still standing at the door.
cells.ask: Pick one small thing that ended and put it away properly this week — the box, the file, the drawer. One thing.
cells.core:
You know what needs to end, and the deciding stopped short of doing it. Since then you've been in the doorway — not in the room on either side — and nothing else gets to start while you stand there. It isn't a clarity problem. The clarity is fine. What's missing is the small physical act of finishing something, so your own decisions start feeling like yours again.

Build one ending from the outside in: the box, the file, the one thing that reads as done when you look at it. Small and real beats sweeping and postponed. Once one thing is actually closed, the next call comes easier, because you'll have the feel of your own hand on it again. Do that one thing.

cells.tense: You keep describing this ending as something that happened to you, while you're the one who keeps choosing the moment.
cells.ask: Tell one person the ending you've been calling unavoidable, and use the word chose. Just once, out loud.
cells.core:
Something is ending around you, and you frame it as if the timing were set by someone else. But the timing has your handwriting on it. You've been keeping the pieces in place while the change runs, and you call that 'just getting through' — as if it were the situation's work, not yours.

That's the part worth owning. The call was made, and the staying with it after was yours too. Keep one thing from what this cleared, on purpose, because you decided to keep it. Saying the deciding once is enough — no speech needed, no defence of it. What you do now is say that the call was yours.
cells.sheetLine: You made this call. You've been calling it no choice.

attempts.check: The record doesn't support 'you know it' — balanced is the capacity working, not the person's awareness of it, so I'll locate the authority in the deciding itself and let them recognise it or not. A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not sure I'm the one deciding' — the ask stands either way: writing the line down is harmless if the read is wrong and useful if it's right. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line telling them they already know; I've cut that and kept the act.
